power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: PRABAT: Test-Retest Reliability of a Pragmatic Abilities Measure
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Hypothesis
The PRABAT total score will demonstrate a significant positive correlation between Time 1 (T1) and Time 2 (T2), indicating good test–retest reliability over a one-week interval. Specifically, the Pearson correlation between PRABAT total scores at T1 and T2 is expected to be statistically significant (p < .05) and at least r ≥ .70.

Null Hypothesis (H0) 
There is no significant correlation between PRABAT scores at T1 and T2. 
Alternative Hypothesis (H1) 
There is a significant correlation between PRABAT scores at T1 and T2. 
 
Research question 
How reliable are the scores of the newly developed PRABAT across two measurement time points separated by approximately one week in typically developing preschool-aged children (3;0–5;11 years)?
table.design_dependent_variables:
The dependent variables are the PRABAT total score at Time 1 (T1) and Time 2 (T2).
For both T1 and T2, the total PRABAT score will be calculated as the sum of correctly answered items.
Responses are recorded automatically via a tablet-based application, and each item is scored dichotomously (1 = correct, 0 = incorrect). Higher total scores indicate better pragmatic language ability.
The same set of PRABAT items and scoring procedures will be used at T1 and T2.
table.study_design_overview: Participants will complete two conditions corresponding to two time points: Time 1 (test) and Time 2 (retest). The study uses a within-subject repeated-measures design, such that all participants take part in both conditions.
table.statistical_tests:
Test–retest reliability will be assessed using Pearson product-moment correlation coefficients. The coefficients will be calculated between T1 and T2 scores for the PRABAT total score. The significance level is α = .05. Additionally, paired-samples t-tests will be conducted to examine whether there are systematic mean differences between T1 and T2. 

Interpretation criteria 
The analysis will use the following thresholds: 
r < .50 = low; .50–.69 = moderate; .70–.89 = good; ≥ .90 = excellent.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants will be excluded from the analyses if they do not complete both testing sessions (T1 and T2), as both measurements are required to assess test–retest reliability. Participants who complete fewer than 16 items in a session will be excluded from the analysis, as their data would not provide a reliable estimate of performance. For each participant and session, the total score will be calculated as the sum of correctly answered items across all valid (non-excluded) items. In addition, participants will be excluded in cases of clear procedural or technical issues (e.g., interruptions during testing, experimenter error, or technical problems with the device) that compromise data quality. No additional exclusion based on statistical outliers is planned.
table.sample_size: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (test family: Exact; statistical test: correlation: bivariate normal model). Assuming an expected correlation of r = .50, α = .05, and power (1 − β) = .95, the required sample size is N = 46. The study will therefore aim to collect data from N = 46 participants. Data collection will continue until this target sample size is reached. Participants will be typically developing children aged between 3;0 and 5;11 years. Recruitment will primarily focus on children aged 3;0–5;0 years; if necessary to reach the target sample size of N = 46, children up to 5;11 years will be included.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 15 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Pragmatic abilities allow us to use and comprehend language in interaction.
The assessment of individual differences in pragmatic abilities, both within and across cultural settings, is crucial to understanding how they develop.
However, tools with good psychometric properties that suit this purpose are lacking.
The current study describes the creation of a test battery assessing individual differences in 3-to 6-year-old children from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds.
The battery is implemented as a tablet-based game, administrable both online and in person.
Children are prompted by a character with one or multiple utterances and respond by selecting a picture among three options on a screen.
An initial larger item pool was piloted in Germany and Kenya to ensure the items' cross-cultural adaptability.
We then used item response modeling on a sample of 713 German children to select items that varied in difficulty and fit the Rasch model.
The so-constructed 19-item battery shows excellent model fit, test-retest reliability and convergent validity.

The way the battery was created allows for easy cross-cultural adaptation, easy administration and scoring, thereby addressing an important gap in the developmental study of the interplay between social cognition and language.
All materials and code are freely accessible to interested researchers.

text.text: Pragmatics, which concerns the use of language in context (Bates, 1976), is a fundamental component of language use and learning.
text.formatted: Pragmatics, which concerns the use of language in context <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bates, 1976)</ref>, is a fundamental component of language use and learning.

text.text: The first theories of pragmatics such as the Gricean Cooperative Principle (Grice, 1975) and Sperber and Wilson's Relevance Theory (1986), adopted a cognitive approach that conceptualized pragmatic processes as inferential processes that integrate literal meaning with information from the context, the speaker and the world.

text.text: Later accounts put more emphasis on the prominent social cognition component of pragmatics, thus seeing pragmatic inferences as social inferences, where Theory of Mind (ToM, or mentalizing), joint attention and perspective playing a crucial role (O'Neill, 2012; Sperber & Wilson, 2002).

text.text: The extent to which pragmatics represents a submodule of, partially or totally overlaps with ToM, is subject of debate.

On the one hand, numerous approaches propose different reconfigurations of pragmatic abilities in relation to social cognition (for some examples, see Andrés-Roqueta & Katsos, 2017 , 2020; Domaneschi & Bambini, 2020; Marocchini & Domaneschi, 2022; O'Neill, 2012; Rubio-Fernandez, 2024).

text.text: On the other hand, more recent approaches, like the Rational Speech Act framework (Degen, 2023), propose a formalization of the traditional conversation principles, thereby operationalizing pragmatic processes as probabilistic, rational inferential processes.

text.text: Despite the flourishing theoretical work, there is no agreed-upon definition of pragmatics and what it encompasses.

This entails a "phenomenological diversity" that makes it difficult to establish whether all phenomena classified as "pragmatic" by different traditions -from implicature, metaphor, irony comprehension to communicative gesture, prosody, turn-taking and politeness understandingactually draw on the same cognitive resources and represent a single, unified construct (Floyd et al., 2025; Matthews, Biney, & Abbot-Smith, 2018; Russell & Grizzle, 2008).

text.text: Empirical research has found pragmatic abilities -differentially conceptualized -to be related to perspective taking, false-belief understanding, vocabulary, grammar, working memory, and inhibitory control (Bambini, Van Looy, Demiddele, & Schaeken, 2021; Matthews et al., 2018) but also mental health (Brenne & Rimehaug, 2019; Dall, Fellinger, & Holzinger, 2022; Law, Rush, Clegg, Peters, & Roulstone, 2015), peer popularity (Gottman, Gonso, & Rasmussen, 1975; Kemple, Speranza, & Hazen, 1992; Law et al., 2015; Law, Rush, & McBean, 2014; Mok, Pickles, Durkin, & Conti-Ramsden, 2014), child prosocial behaviour (Conti-Ramsden et al., 2019), social, emotional and behavioural difficulties (Helland, Lundervold, Heimann, & Posserud, 2014; Murphy, Faulkner, & Farley, 2014; St Clair, Pickles, Durkin, & Conti-Ramsden, 2011), relationship formation (Whitehouse, Watt, Line, & Bishop, 2009), and employability (Eaves & Ho, 2008; Lewis, Woodyatt, & Murdoch, 2008).

text.text: While the clear presence of a link between pragmatics and other domains -first and foremost language, social cognition, executive functions -underscores the importance of this ability for human development and wellbeing, there is a scarcity of psychometrically valid, reliable, individual differences assessment tools for pragmatic abilities (Matthews et al., 2018).

text.text: Being able to track individual differences is crucial in order to understand its development and identify what determines pragmatic development, its variation and how this variation can in turn affect the development of other cognitive and social abilities (Matthews et al., 2018).

text.text: In order to build universal theories about development, it is important to have a database that represents the diversity of human experience beyond traditionally overstudied populations from the Global North because pragmatic skills are tightly connected to culturally variable factors such as language and social norms (Levinson, 1983).

text.text: Research at the level of individualdifferences can help achieve this goal (Levinson, 2012): it allows to verify whether the relationship between two variables (e.g., a cognitive trait and an aspect of experience, or the development of two different abilities) holds consistently both within and across cultural groups (Bohn, Fong, Pope-Caldwell, Stengelin, & Haun, 2024).

text.text: The cross-cultural applicability is largely neglected in assessment tools for pragmatic abilities.
Even though a multitude of pragmatic assessment tools exist, there is a need for comprehensive measures of individual differences, in particular for young children (Matthews et al., 2018).

text.text: A large portion of assessment tools were designed with a diagnostic/screening goal for a broad range of populations: from adults to children, from populations with developmental language disorders (CSBS-DP, Wetherby & Prizant, 2002; ESCS, Mundy et al., 2003), autism spectrum disorder (Pragma, Loukusa, Mäkinen, Gabbatore, Laukkanen-Nevala, & Leinonen, 2017; CCC-2, Bishop, 2006; YiPP, Simmons, Paul, & Volkmar, 2014; SEE, Wiig, 2008; ADOS, Lord et al., 2000), neurodevelopmental disorders (PleaseApp, Andrés-Roqueta, Flores Buils, & Igualada, 2024), attention (POM, Cordier, Munro, Wilkes-Gillan, Speyer, & Pearce, 2014) and social-pragmatics deficits (CCC-2, Bishop, 2006; LUI, O'Neill, 2007; PLSI, Gilliam & Miller, 2006) to brain injuries, neuropsychological and psychiatric disorders (ABaCo, Sacco et al., 2008; APACS, Arcara & Bambini, 2016).

text.text: Most of the tests for children rely on a narrative structure and/or meta-cognitive approaches, by requiring children to either respond to or explain specific types of statements or stimuli.
Alternatively, indirect measures such as checklists and questionnaires are used, where parents, clinicians, or experts answer questions based on previous observations of the child.

Other instruments include either semi-structured interviews between the clinician and the child, or observations of unstructured interactions between the child and peers or adults during, e.g., play and school contexts, in some cases via time-sampling techniques (for an overview of the available instruments grouped according to this tentative classification, see Table 1).

text.text: However, they present multiple disadvantages.

As the observation of undisturbed interactions may provide the most naturalistic setting to assess a child's pragmatic abilities, this method requires, most of the time, highly trained personnel to conduct the assessment and is considerably time-consuming [not only for the time of the assessment, ranging from 20 (POM, Cordier et al., 2014) to 30 minutes (CSBS-DP, Wetherby & Prizant, 2002; PP, Prutting & Kittchner, 1987), but also for the scoring itself, which can last up to 60-75 minutes in the case of the CSBS-DP].

text.text: This problem is partially overcome by tasks that require children to respond to verbal prompts and reason about scenarios and conversations (Pragma, Loukusa et al., 2017; CASL, Carrow-Woolfolk, 2017; TOPL-2, Phelps-Terasaki & Phelps-Gunn, 2007).

text.text: These instruments usually take less time and minimize the scoring length.
However, they still require considerable control of attention, memory, and meta-cognitive skills that younger children may not have.

Checklists and questionnaires completed by adult caregivers, in turn, eliminate this problem and allow to gain information about younger samples (Bishop, 2006; O'Neill, 2007), which would be hardly testable with tools requiring elaborate responses to verbal prompts.

text.text: At the same time, by involving adults they sacrifice direct assessment of the child's pragmatic abilitiesand thus, ecological validity (O'Neill, 2014).

Moreover, it is often difficult to determine who is the "most informed respondent": first, because, as children start going to school, neither parents nor teachers may be able to give the full picture of the child's communicative ability (O'Neill, 2014); second, because there is considerable cross-cultural variation in how many people are involved in the upbringing of a child (e.g., in Kenya, the rearing of the children involves extended family members as well, Oburu, 2024).

text.text: To our knowledge, there is only one example of a digital assessment tool that children can complete by themselves, namely the PleaseApp (Andrés-Roqueta et al., 2024).

text.text: The PleaseApp instrument is a game application where 5-to 11-year-old children go through multiple scenarios, each involving the evaluation of different aspects of receptive pragmatic abilities, such as understanding of figurative language, narrative, referential expressions, indirect speech acts, humor, gesture-speech integration and politeness.
The presence of text and the complexity of the tasks, however, makes the test not suitable for younger children.

Nonetheless, as the authors underline, digital assessment tools offer a great opportunity to control for contextual factors, fundamental in pragmatic abilities' assessment, and can be administered both online and in person, increasing the probability to reach the desired sample size (the lack of which is often a problem when doing correlational research, Matthews et al., 2018).

text.text: In this paper, we present the development of a psychometrically reliable and valid, easilyadministrable tool that can assess individual differences in different pragmatic abilities in multiple cultural settings and languages in the preschool age (i.e., 3-to 6-year-old children).
For its development we took the following steps.
First, we created a large pool of items assessing a broad range of pragmatic abilities.

In order to establish precise criteria about which items to include, we specified a working definition of pragmatic phenomena based on previous literature (Grice, 1975; O'Neill, 2012; Sperber & Wilson, 1986).
text.formatted: In order to establish precise criteria about which items to include, we specified a working definition of pragmatic phenomena based on previous literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Grice, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">O'Neill, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Sperber & Wilson, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: For our purpose, an item requires pragmatic reasoning to be solved when: 1) the item contains either a literal linguistic or paralinguistic message that is not sufficient in order to comprehend the intended meaning of the utterance; 2) to be correctly interpreted, the literal linguistic or paralinguistic message needs to be integrated with information either about the interlocutor, about the world, or about the context (see Appendix A for a list of items and how each one reflects these criteria) 1 .
In order for the instrument to be objective and brief, we developed it as a digital application that could be administered both in person and online.

This not only ensures consistency of variables such as conversational context and intonation, but also allows for easy administration -not requiring specialized personnel such as clinicians and speech therapists -and therefore facilitates achieving larger sample sizes.

Because modern technologies do not (yet) allow for immediate and accurate transcription of audio (production) data, we focused on the assessment of receptive pragmatic abilities, a still understudied domain of pragmatics (Andrés-Roqueta et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Because modern technologies do not (yet) allow for immediate and accurate transcription of audio (production) data, we focused on the assessment of receptive pragmatic abilities, a still understudied domain of pragmatics <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Andrés-Roqueta et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Because we wanted our test battery to be cross-culturally adaptable, we only included items that could be easily adapted to multiple cultures in a comparable way.

To ensure that, we consulted with native speakers from Kenya, Türkiye, and Germany (the three contexts the battery was initially developed for, see section on Cross-cultural adaptation), and only included items that were judged appropriate across these three -culturally and linguistically distinct -contexts.

For example, irony and sarcasm comprehension were left out, as the adaptation of such an item would require substantial changes to the task depending on the culture with little certainty about its cross-cultural comparability.
We then used Item Response (IRT) models to select the bestperforming items from the initial pool to ensure that items measure the same latent ability.
More precisely, we aimed for the battery to conform to a 1-parameter logistic (1PL; Rasch) model, so that the sum score can be used as a score for performance (Rasch, 1960).

text.text: Although factorial work is much needed to investigate the potential heterogeneous nature of pragmatics (Floyd et al.,   1 It is important to note that our goal here is not to give a definition of pragmatic ability, but rather to define operationalizable and concrete criteria that help us in defining what should be included as pragmatic phenomena.
2025), IRT is well suited for test construction, as it allows to build item sets by looking at the probability to solve an item as a function of the underlying ability and item-level estimates.

Whereas other latent-variable approaches as, e.g., exploratory factor analysis (EFA) investigate how many latent dimensions account for shared variance between items, our goal was not to identify the different dimensions characterizing pragmatics; rather, we aimed at building a battery consisting of items that function well along a common pragmatic-ability continuum and that allowed us to distinguish with precision individuals with different pragmatic ability levels.
Additionally, we aimed for a final battery that contained items that not only best measure the latent pragmatic ability, but that can also capture individual differences.

In order to achieve both these goals, we used a semi-automated selection procedure to find a subset of items that both conformed to a Rasch model and contained items spread across the latent ability scale.
Finally, in order to ensure the psychometric quality of the instrument, we looked at differential item functioning, and assessed the test -retest reliability and convergent validity.
In the following sections, we report the construction, psychometric evaluation, and crosscultural adaptation of this measurement tool, which we call PraBat (Pragmatics test Battery).
In the initial item pool, we aimed at including items assessing as broad a range of pragmatic abilities as possible.

However, in order to obtain a battery characterized by a simple administration procedure and easy cross-cultural adaptability, items had to meet specific criteria: • they had to be implementable in a picture selection paradigm, to avoid a narrative task structure, and effortful scoring procedure; items therefore had to assess a receptive pragmatic ability, as the paradigm did not allow to test for expressive abilities; • items should not require culture or language specific background knowledge (see Cultural adaptation section for details); and they had to target pragmatic abilities developing between 3 and 6 years of age.

The test battery was implemented as an interactive picture book in HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
It was programmed as a Progressive Web App and can thus be run online as a website in any browser but can also be downloaded and run offline if needed.

The battery begins with a short sequence of images where Ella introduces herself, her family, and friends.

IRT models describe the probability to solve an item with a logistic function that takes into account the person's ability level and specific item parameters.
This function is best represented by Item Characteristic Curves, which show the probability to solve an item given a specific ability level.
ICCs can also be used to visually inspect the parameter estimates of different items not only in relation to one another, but also in relation to the latent ability in question.

For example, an item's curve position along the x axis is determined by its difficulty, while an item's curve steepness is determined by how precisely that item discriminates between individuals with different ability levels, i.e. the item's discrimination: a highly discriminating item differentiates more strongly between individuals with slightly different ability levels around the item's difficulty, resulting in a steeper ICC.

text.text: The sum score can be used as a sufficient test score only if the items conform to the Rasch model: across the entire latent ability, the model assumes that the probability to solve an easier item will never be lower than the probability to solve a more difficult item.
This assumption does not hold in the case of 2PL models.
2PL models would therefore need the test results to be fit into the model in order to estimate the person's ability level, thus requiring norming data and a scoring model.
A Rasch compliant battery is therefore a better solution for easy and immediate scoring.
For each item, we quantified its fit to the Rasch model in the following way: first, we extracted item fit statistics, i.e.
Infit and Outfit.
These statistics indicate the fit of the individual items to the model.

While Infit focuses on the model's performance when the person's ability level is at the item's target difficulty level, the Outfit describes the model's performance when the person's ability level is far from the item's target difficulty level, thus being more sensitive to outliers.
These statistics are calculated for each item and should have a value between 0.7 and 1.3 (Wright & Linacre, 1994).
text.formatted: These statistics are calculated for each item and should have a value between 0.7 and 1.3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Wright & Linacre, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Second, we extracted the discrimination parameters for each item from the 2PL model.
In order to build a battery containing items that well fit a Rasch model, it is necessary for the main assumptions to be satisfied.
Items with very similar discrimination parameters are items that together will give a better Rasch model fit.
Lastly, in order to have a battery that allows us to look at individual differences, a sufficient number of items covering a wide range of the target latent ability are necessary.
From the Rasch model, we extracted easiness (inverse of difficulty) parameters, as to know how items are distributed along the latent ability scale.
The next step was to use the statistics we extracted and use them to determine the best subset of items.
To do that, we formulated an objective function that would calculate a score for each subset of items based on the infit, outfit, easiness, and discrimination parameters of the contained items.

The objective function's purpose was to penalize subsets that did not reflect the following criteria: contained Rasch compliant items; contained items equally spread across the latent ability scale; contained items that had similar discrimination parameters.
These requirements were quantified in the following way.
The score for easiness spacing was calculated as the standard deviation of the distance between difficulty estimates of adjacent estimates.
Items were sorted by difficulty, and the distance was calculated as the difference between difficulty estimates of adjacent items.
A lower score indicated a lower standard deviation of the difficulty spacing between items, namely closer-to-equal easiness spacing between the subset's items.
This score was then divided by three to bring it to a scale comparable to the other components.
To score Infit and Outfit, we calculated the average of the distance of each item's fit value from 1.
This average was then multiplied by -4 in the case of Infit and -2 in the case of Outfit.
More weight was therefore given to bad Infit values.
Lastly, the discrimination score was determined as the variance of the subset items' discrimination parameters multiplied by -6.
These four scores were summed together resulting in an always negative total score.
More negative values therefore indicated a lower, i.e. worse score.
The objective function's score would then be used inside a simulated annealing (SA) algorithm (Kirkpatrick, Gelatt, & Vecchi, 1983).
text.formatted: The objective function's score would then be used inside a simulated annealing (SA) algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Kirkpatrick, Gelatt, & Vecchi, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: The SA algorithm is a probabilistic optimization procedure that, in our case, returns the best item combination for each subset size.

For each subset size considered, the algorithm does the following: it starts from a randomly determined subset of items; randomly substitutes items of that subset; if the objective function returns a better value than before, the newly proposed subset becomes the starting point for the successive proposals.
A "temperature" parameter influences the probability of the algorithm to accept a specific proposal.

In the initial "hot" phase, where the temperature parameter is high, the process accepts more often proposals that decrease the objective function's score, preventing the algorithm from getting stuck in local optima (best subset within a neighboring set of choices) and facilitating the discovery of global optima (best subsets overall).
As the temperature decreases, the probability of accepting lower scored subsets decreases, favoring the acceptance of better proposals.
This allows for the refinement of the best subset found during the hot phase.

Because we did not want to have a battery containing less than 18 items (as to cover the latent ability range with enough precision) and because we already knew at least two to three items had very bad parameters and/or fit, we let the SA algorithm iterate over 18-to 23-item subset sizes.

Once the simulated annealing algorithm identified the best subset for each subset size, we assessed whether the Rasch model provides an acceptable fit both in absolute terms and relative to a 2PL model.

In the current study, we presented the development of PraBat, a test battery to assess individual differences in pragmatic abilities in preschool children from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds.
We initially compiled a larger item pool of pragmatic tasks based on the literature.

We then used Item Response models in combination with a semi-automated selection algorithm, to identify a set of items that best balanced between an overall good fit to the Rasch model and a set size that allows differentiating between individuals.
The result is a 19-item battery which displayed good test-retest reliability and convergent validity.
Out of the 27 items in the initial item pool, 8 were excluded.

One might wonder what the exclusion of these items means for the questions of which items -and with that which procedures or inferences -should be considered part of the broader concept of pragmatics.
The fact that specific items were not included in the final battery does not necessarily negate their pragmatic nature and should be seen in light of how items were selected.
The selection was guided by an algorithm that maximized an objective function which balanced between variability in item difficulty, item discrimination, and fit to the Rasch model.
Therefore, the reasons for the exclusion of specific tasks are manifold.
Some items, for example, had good discrimination and fit, but were very similar in difficulty to other items which had an overall better profile.
This was the case for the items Listener conversational perspective taking 1 and 2, and Communicative gesture comprehension 3.
Other items were excluded because they showed a poor outfit (Metaphor Adjective) or low discrimination (Conversational Implicature 1, Informativeness 1, see Figure 1 in Supplementary Material).

text.text: While poor outfit (the only item-level fit issue present in our items, see Figure 2 in Supplementary Material) may indicate too high predictability of the responses and may be due to the high easiness of the items (Boone, Staver, & Yale, 2014; Linacre, 2002; Wright & Linacre, 1994), low discrimination values indicate that a specific item does not differentiate well between different sections of the latent ability, but not that the supposedly measured ability is not pragmatic.

text.text: For example, low discrimination value for Informativeness 1 may have been determined by the heavy load of the task on memory skills, while performance in Conversational Implicature 1 may have been influenced by the ambiguous nature of the prompt sentence.

However, other items capturing the same phenomena (Informativeness 2 and Conversational Implicature 2) showed better discrimination estimates, indicating that different versions of the same items, relying less on memory and on less ambiguous sentences, succeeded in differentiating between sections of the latent ability.

Scalar Implicature and Verb Mutual Exclusivity on the contrary, were very difficult items that were probably excluded due to their high difficulty compared to the rest of the items, and would not have guaranteed sensitivity to individual differences for higher ability levels: the objective function penalizes item subsets where the deviation of the average easiness distance between adjacent items is high; therefore, subsets including these two items, being very far in difficulty from the rest of the items, were penalized by the objective function.
PraBat has several advantages that make it an important addition to the toolkit for investigating pragmatic abilities.
First, the battery shows very good psychometric qualities, in particular good test-retest reliability and convergent validity.
On the practical side, it is implemented as a web app that can be used both remotely and in person.
This allows for easy data collection, with no need of manual coding, transcriptions, and trained personnel.
The good fit to the Rasch model allows for easy scoring because the sum score serves as a sufficient statistic (Rasch, 1960).

text.text: Moreover, children can complete the final battery in approximately 5 to 10 minutes.

These two features address the resource issues that most of the pragmatic assessment tools have, allowing to potentially reach bigger samples needed for individual differences research (Matthews et al., 2018).

text.text: PraBat's practicality additionally applies to its cultural and linguistic adaptability.
The interface was designed to be appropriate for multiple cultural contexts.

More importantly, the items have been thought to be suitable for three very different linguistic and cultural contexts (Germany, Türkiye and Kenya) from the start: the included items therefore comprised only phenomena that, for their resolution, require context, speaker, and world information potentially available to children from different cultures and speaking different languages.
Therefore, all items can potentially be adapted and translated to a vast range of cultures and languages without major changes.
Despite the benefits of the final battery, there are also several limitations.

First, there are important pragmatic phenomena which could not be included, such as, for example, politeness and humor, which highly rely on cultural aspects, other more language-specific phenomena that involve, e.g., reference assignment, interpretation of definite and indefinite articles, determiners and pronouns, intonation patterns marking information structure, pragmatic particles.
As already mentioned, these phenomena were excluded to ensure the cross-cultural appropriateness of the battery.
Secondly, we are aware of the fact that, despite careful adaptation and translation, there might be fine-grained pragmatic aspects that can change from one context to another.

Apart from the linguistic nuances that might be an inevitable and direct consequence of translation, culture might also have an influence on the priority with which specific kinds of information are being considered when solving an item.
Additionally, whether the result of IRT measurement models are valid for other cultural contexts -i.e., if they are invariant -needs to be further investigated (Kachergis et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Additionally, whether the result of IRT measurement models are valid for other cultural contexts -i.e., if they are invariant -needs to be further investigated <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Kachergis et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, we believe our battery can be appreciated as one of the first committed efforts to minimize the impact of cross-cultural differences on assessment of pragmatic abilities.

Despite these limitations, we still argue that the performance in this battery, be it receptive, applied in interaction with an animated character, and possibly subject to fine-grained cross-linguistic and cross-cultural differences, can be indicative of children's general pragmatic ability.

Nonetheless, future research aiming at untangling the nature of pragmatic abilities could create more items measuring the excluded abilities as, e.g., scalar implicatures and conversational perspective taking, and verify whether their fit indices and parameters change.
For example, we believe the use of the quantifier "einige" (german translation of "some") might have contributed to the high difficulty of the scalar implicature item.

Investigating the fit of a scalar implicature involving another quantifier might reveal whether scalar implicatures per se constitute other forms of meaning enrichment not represented in the pragmatic continuum assessed in this battery (e.g., explicatures, Noveck & Sperber, 2007).

PraBat represents an important step forward in pragmatic research, as it addresses the need of easily administrable tools that can provide high-quality assessment of individual differences.
We believe this instrument represents an important tool for any researcher investigating pragmatic abilities and how these relate to other social-cognitive abilities or life experiences.
